item.title: Five strikes, 34 tanks hit—Ukraine keeps coming back to the same Russian oil hub
item.summary: Satellite images show 34 oil tanks destroyed or damaged at Russia's Samara pumping hub after five Ukrainian drone strikes, Ukrainian OSINT project ...
item.page_text:
Satellite images show 34 oil tanks destroyed or damaged at Russia’s Samara pumping hub after five Ukrainian drone strikes, Ukrainian OSINT project Dnipro Osint reported . The latest , overnight on 2 November, also led Kazakhstan to temporarily stop oil flows through the Atyrau–Samara pipeline.
The station sits near the village of Prosvet in Samara Oblast. Russia blends crude from different fields there into Urals, its main export grade. Since spring, Ukraine has aimed what Ukrainian officials call “long-range sanctions” at the pumps and pipes that carry Russian oil to market. In May alone, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry counted 18 Russian oil facilities struck. Samara shows that method focused on a single node, hit again and again within a month.
Dnipro Osint published the images on 8 November. Containers shielded some of the station’s equipment and probably helped limit the damage, the channel added. The 34 tanks are nearly half of the station’s 71.
Radio Svoboda’s Russian service, which obtained satellite images on 8 November, found that up to 10 tanks had burned out completely. Smoke was still rising from one of them six days after the latest strike, the outlet wrote . Earlier, Ukraine’s General Staff said the 7 October strike alone destroyed four tanks of 50,000 cubic meters each.
Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry said that oil intake through the Atyrau–Samara pipeline was temporarily suspended on the morning of 2 November because of the drone attack. Ministry spokesperson Asel Serikpayeva said oil was again moving normally through the pipeline as of 3 November, after a technical inspection.
Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev claimed that Russian forces downed 46 drones over the region that night. He did not mention damage to oil facilities, The Insider noted . Atyrau–Samara is Kazakhstan’s second-largest oil export route after the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, and both rely on Russian infrastructure, The Times of Central Asia reported .

item.title: Blowing in the Wind
item.summary: There is something undeniably romantic about casting a message in a bottle into the ocean. After all, what could be more enchanting than surrendering a personal secret to the tides, with nothing but the hope that it might one day wash ashore and find its way into a stranger's hands? Tell the Sky takes this idea to the skies. However with this interactive map, instead of throwing a bottle into the ocean, you write a message on a glowing virtual lantern and release it into the wind. Carried by real-world wind currents, your lantern drifts across the world until someone catches it, reads your message and adds one of their own before sending it on its way again. The map visualizes global wind patterns with animated streams flowing around the planet. But these aren't just decorative weather conditions. They determine where your lantern travels. Launch a lantern and it will be carried along by the prevailing winds, potentially travelling across continents and oceans before another user has an opportunity to catch it. item.page_text:
By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement , Privacy Policy , and Cookie Policy .
Day 9 of the #30DayMapChallenge , theme: Urban-Rural.

In Spain we call it “la España vaciada”, the emptied Spain, which are the villages of the interior that lost most of their people in a few decades. Watch it happen census by census, from 1857 until today!

Each municipality is coloured by how many people live in each km², from pale (almost nobody) to dark red (the cities).

Some things I found while putting it together:
- Until 1950 the map barely changes. Cuenca reached its highest population ever that year, 344,033 people.
- Between 1960 and 1981 it all happens at once. Móstoles, next to Madrid, went from 2,578 people in 1960 to 150,259 in 1981.
- Soria, Teruel and Cuenca now have 42 to 49 % fewer people than at their peak.
- In 1950 only 64 municipalities had fewer than 100 people. Today there are 1,406.
- Spain as a whole has more than three times the people it had in 1857, from 15.5 to 49 million.

Why it happened:
- The 1959 Stabilization Plan helped accelerate Spain's economic transformation, and industrial jobs expanded around Madrid, Barcelona, Bilbao and Valencia.
- At the same time, tractors and other machinery were transforming agriculture, so farms needed fewer workers.
- So people left, especially the young. Many moved to industrial cities or their growing suburbs, like Móstoles. Others emigrated abroad, particularly to France, Germany and Switzerland.
- And when young people leave, fewer children are born. Many villages kept shrinking long after the great rural exodus had ended.

How it was made:
- Population: every census from 1857 to 1991 from mapSpainHist by Pau Vall Prat (CC BY 4.0), with the boundaries each municipality had in each census, and the INE yearly register (Padrón) from 1996 to 2025. The years in between are interpolated.
- Terrain: Copernicus GLO-30 read at 60 m.
- Render: Blender 5.2. #30DayMapChallenge #Blender #Spain #Demography #DataVisualization #GIS #OpenData

item.title: Exploring the world's languages with Language Explorer
item.page_text:
Daan van Esch, Senior Technical Program Manager, Google DeepMind and Uche Okonkwo, Senior Program Manager, Google Research
Language Explorer, featured in an exhibition at the Museum of Communication in Berlin, Germany, lets you explore the world's linguistic diversity online through visualizations and data.
Our world has a fascinating wealth of languages, and for over two decades, Google has been building language technologies that cover as many languages as possible. In 2006, we started a small experiment with Google Translate, supporting just two languages (English and Arabic) at the time. Fast forward to today: nearly 250 languages are supported, with around a trillion words translated every month . Our commitment to linguistic diversity runs across products, all in service of our mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. Building products that reflect the world's linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that's deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. This is why we've been working on grassroots initiatives like Project Vaani in India and Project Waxal in Africa, partnering with local organizations to collect thousands of hours of open speech data across underserved languages.
But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties.
To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we've been working on a tool to help visualize the world's linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Developed as part of our 1,000 Languages Initiative , the Language Explorer brings together data across thousands of languages, building on our open-source LinguaMeta dataset .
This week marks the opening of a new major exhibition at the Museum of Communication Berlin, Real Talk! Language. Power. World. ( Real Talk! Sprache. Macht. Welt. ) featuring the Language Explorer as an interactive installation. The exhibition explores how language shapes identity, society, and technology across a multi-year run in Berlin (through February 2028) and at the Museum of Communication Frankfurt (through September 2029). The Language Explorer installation reflects our broader work to build AI and language technologies that serve everyone, regardless of what language they speak, read, or sign .
If you can't make it to the exhibition in person, you can explore the museum's themes via an online companion starting November 6th, or dive directly into the world's rich linguistic diversity online with the Language Explorer .

item.title: Iran distributes iodine near nuclear site ahead of possible U.S. strike — The Times
item.summary: A satellite image shows tunnel entrances at ...
item.page_text:
Iranian authorities are preparing residents for possible
U.S. strikes on a nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain, distributing iodine
tablets to people living within 2–3 kilometers (1.2–1.9 miles) of potential
targets to protect them from radiation exposure.
An Iranian Health Ministry official described the
preparations to The
Times , saying similar measures are taken during every war.
Authorities are focusing particular attention on the
underground complex beneath Pickaxe Mountain, also known as Kolang Gaz La. The
mountain is located near the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, which the
United States attacked in June 2025.
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to
strike the underground complex, whose precise purpose has yet to be
established. He most recently raised the possibility on Oct. 31, stressing that
the United States needed to “take care of Pickaxe Mountain” and that the U.S.
military could do so very quickly.
“Yes, we are distributing iodine. Trump can no longer be
trusted. He really could commit this crime,” the Iranian Health Ministry
official said.
Iranian authorities have also begun circulating
instructional videos on local social media platforms explaining what residents
should do in the event of a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain. Residents
are advised to stay indoors, avoid going outside and monitor official announcements.
The videos also warn that the destruction of the underground
complex could release radioactive soil and rock particles into the atmosphere.
In that event, residents of nearby communities would have only 10–15 minutes
before dangerous radioactive dust reached them.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called on the United
States to end hostilities on all fronts on Nov. 8, warning that Tehran was
prepared to respond to further escalation. He stressed that Iran’s two-day
proposal remained in effect.
“Our two-day proposal remains in effect: Meet the demands,
including ending the war on all fronts, and you will see the result. Or choose
war — and watch our vigilant, battle-hardened warriors unleash hell on you,”
Araghchi said.
Axios reported on Nov. 3 that Trump was considering three
options for the war with Iran: reaching a peace agreement, resuming hostilities
or applying economic pressure. Trump has maintained that he is in no hurry to
make a decision.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Oct. 23, Trump said the
United States could
conduct another military operation against Iran . Two days later, ahead of Israel’s
parliamentary elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released an AI-generated
image depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv and warned of the threat of a
“second Holocaust” if Iran acquired nuclear weapons.
Axios journalist Barak Ravid, citing a U.S. official,
reported that following the Republicans’ showing in the midterm elections, Trump
could become more willing to authorize a large-scale military operation against
Iran.
The military war may be swinging in our favor, but the information war continues.
Just as an army needs soldiers, so does a free society need its journalists to ensure that people have access to honest, trustworthy voices to understand the world around them.
For the past five years, The New Voice of Ukraine has been working tirelessly to push back against Russian narratives and defend democracy. But we cannot do it alone.
